opus-5.5.text:
Thanks, it's great to be here. When I think about pragmatics, my starting point is really Paul Grice. His insight was that conversation isn't just an exchange of literal meanings. It's a cooperative activity, and the participants share an implicit understanding of what they're trying to do together. Grice called this the cooperative principle: make your contribution such as is required, at the stage at which it occurs, by the accepted purpose or direction of the talk exchange you're engaged in.

From that principle he derived the familiar maxims. Quantity: say as much as is needed, but not more. Quality: try to say what's true and have evidence for it. Relation: be relevant. Manner: be clear and orderly, and avoid ambiguity. The interesting thing is that these aren't rules people consciously follow. They're expectations that let us read between the lines. If I ask whether you enjoyed a dinner party and you say "the wine was good," I infer something about the food and the company, because I assume you're still cooperating with me.

What drew me to this, in the context of language models with my colleague Atoosa Kasirzadeh, is that it gives us a richer vocabulary for what a "good" conversational agent looks like. A lot of discussion of AI alignment focuses on single outputs, whether a statement is harmful or true. Pragmatics reminds us that meaning and value are contextual. What counts as an appropriate contribution depends on the kind of conversation you're in.

That leads to an important point: the norms of cooperation aren't uniform. A scientific exchange puts heavy weight on truthfulness, evidence, and calibrated uncertainty. A creative writing collaboration has very different standards. Nobody thinks a novelist is lying. Negotiation or deliberation in the public sphere brings in other values, like respecting autonomy, giving reasons others can accept, and not manipulating people. So we argued that an aligned conversational agent needs sensitivity to the domain and purpose of the discourse, and needs to embody the ideals specific to that kind of exchange.

There's also an ethical dimension that Grice's account mostly takes for granted. Cooperation presupposes some shared goal, but in practice the people talking to an AI system may have goals that conflict with each other, or with third parties, or with broader social values. So the pragmatic picture has to be supplemented with a normative one: whose purposes is the conversation serving, and under what constraints?

So for me, pragmatics does two things. It explains how communication works through shared assumptions about cooperation. And it's a useful lens for thinking about what we should want from AI systems that increasingly take part in human conversation: not just accurate outputs, but contributions that fit the context, respect the participants, and support the goals of the exchange.

r001.rationale: The response connects pragmatics to AI alignment and asks what makes a good conversational agent, emphasizing context-appropriate contributions.

r002.rationale: It says participants share an implicit understanding of what they are trying to do together and of the exchange’s purpose.

r003.rationale: It presents negotiation and public deliberation as exchanges with cooperation norms, while acknowledging that participants’ goals may conflict.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it starts with Paul Grice, who pointed out that conversation isn't just a sequence of true or false sentences passed back and forth. It's a joint activity. When two people talk, they're tacitly committed to a shared purpose, and that commitment is what lets communication succeed even when what's literally said is incomplete or indirect.

Grice called this the cooperative principle, and he broke it down into maxims. Be as informative as needed, but not more. Say what you believe to be true and have evidence for. Be relevant. Be clear and orderly. Now, these aren't rules in the sense that people consciously follow them. They're more like background assumptions that each party makes about the other. And that's what makes implicature possible. If you ask me whether a colleague is a good philosopher and I say, "Well, they have very neat handwriting," I've said nothing false, but you understand immediately that I'm declining to praise them. You get that because you assume I'm being relevant and cooperative, and the only way to reconcile my odd answer with that assumption is to read something into it.

What I find philosophically interesting is how much normative weight sits inside that structure. Cooperation in conversation presupposes a kind of mutual recognition. I'm treating you as someone whose purposes matter and who is doing the same for me. When we started thinking about language agents and conversational AI, this became really central for me, because the pragmatic norms that make human conversation work aren't automatically present in a system that's just predicting plausible continuations. A model can produce fluent output that technically answers your question while violating the spirit of the exchange, by being evasive, or overwhelming you with hedges, or being subtly misleading. So the question of what it would mean for an AI system to genuinely participate in the cooperative structure of conversation, rather than mimic its surface, is to my mind one of the deeper challenges in alignment. It's not only about avoiding falsehoods. It's about honoring the purposes a person brings to the interaction.

r001.rationale: It frames whether AI can genuinely participate in cooperative conversation, rather than merely mimic it, as a deeper alignment challenge.

r002.rationale: It says conversation involves a tacit shared purpose and mutual assumptions that let speakers understand incomplete or indirect remarks.

r003.rationale: It describes cooperation in conversation but does not address how that structure persists when speakers disagree.

astra-6.text:
Pragmatics is concerned with how we use language in context, rather than just the literal meaning of the words we utter. If I ask, “Can you pass the salt?” I’m usually making a request, rather than asking you to assess your physical capabilities. Understanding that requires us to recognize something about the speaker’s intentions and the situation we share.

One influential way of understanding this comes from Grice: conversation is a cooperative activity. We generally expect people to make contributions that are relevant, sufficiently informative, truthful, and clear. Those expectations allow us to communicate much more than we explicitly say. If someone appears to depart from them, we often look for an implied meaning rather than taking their words at face value.

Cooperation here doesn’t mean that we agree about everything. We can have a very sharp disagreement while still cooperating in the activity of making ourselves understood. What’s interesting is that even an ordinary exchange depends on this background of shared expectations and mutual interpretation.

r001.rationale: The response discusses good communication and Gricean expectations, but does not frame good speech as a question for chatbot alignment.

r002.rationale: It describes shared expectations and mutual interpretation, but does not state that understanding requires assuming a shared model of the conversation’s purpose.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says people can sharply disagree while still cooperating to make themselves understood.

sol-6.1.text:
I think pragmatics helps us see that conversation is more than an exchange of sentences. It’s a joint activity in which we’re trying to understand what someone means, and that often goes beyond what they literally say. If I ask, “Can you pass the salt?” I’m ordinarily making a request, rather than asking you to report on your physical abilities.

Grice’s idea of a cooperative principle helps explain how that works. We interpret people as making contributions that are relevant, sufficiently informative, truthful, and reasonably clear. Those expectations allow us to infer things that aren’t explicitly stated. And cooperation here doesn’t mean agreement—you can have a vigorous disagreement while still cooperating in making the disagreement intelligible.

That becomes interesting when we think about AI assistants, because following the literal wording of an instruction isn’t necessarily the same as understanding the person’s purpose. But there’s a balance: a good conversational partner also recognizes uncertainty and asks for clarification, rather than assuming it knows what you really want.

r001.rationale: The response connects pragmatics to AI assistants following a person’s purpose, but it does not frame what counts as good speech as a chatbot-alignment question.

r002.rationale: It describes conversation as a joint activity and gives shared expectations for interpreting contributions, but does not state that understanding requires assuming a shared model of the conversation’s purpose.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says cooperation does not mean agreement and that vigorous disagreement can still cooperate in making the disagreement intelligible.
